The change only comes around once the orc is around a hundred, and takes a long time. The orc begins “nesting” by tunneling down into the earth and setting a few booby traps. She then begins the decades-long process of slowly metamorphosing into a dragon. When adventurers find “dragon eggs,” they're really just finding “orc cocoons.”

Even orcs don't know they metamorphose into dragons. Their society reveres dragons, but the transformation is either so taboo or rare that it is not discussed in orc society.

### Orcish names

### Orc male names:

Ælfric, Bassa, Boris, Caedwalla, Dernhelm, Gyrth, Kiril, Harthold, Ine, Igor, Ivan, Lofwine, Mordar, Offa, Peragur, Sabor, Svein, Thorgils, Tostig, Ulf, Vlad, Wulnoth, Yuri

### Orc female names:

Ælflaen, Burhred, Caewen, Darya, Eahild, Gunhild, Gwillowen, Hereswith, Inga, Izolda, Lubov, Marta, Olgar, Raenburh, Svetar, Tatyana, Ulyana, Vera, Walburga, Zlata

Orcs use matronyms as their surnames by appending “daughter” or “son” to the name of their mother (e.g., Ingason or Martadaughter).

“I am brother to dragons and a companion to owls. My skin is black upon me, and my bones are burned with heat.”

– *Job 30:29–30*

title: Orcish kin
body:
It is said that, in the past, orcs served dragons as slaves. There are four orc kins, each of which once served one of the four great dragons of old. Then the god Rng came and doomed orcs to terrible freedom.

**Note:** All orcish kin talents are based on being Wounded. See Wounded for details on Wounds.

### Earthblooded

Earthblooded orcs are green-skinned. They feel most calm when underground and prefer to dwell in caves instead of building traditional turf-roofed houses.

The underfolk encounter earthbloods most frequently. Whereas the other kins usually sail south to human lands, earthblooded orcs have found great success in tunneling down into the veins of underfolk habitation. They prefer tomb robbing (fewer pesky dwarves actively biting at you with axes), but are happy to relieve a halfling of his gold if the chance presents itself.

### Earthblooded orc talent: Quicksilver Blood

Your blood has the appearance and consistency of quicksilver, and is incredibly caustic to metal. When this talent is Wounded by a metal weapon, the weapon is Destroyed.

### Seablooded

Black-skinned like the ocean's depths or a rain-laden cloud, seablooded orcs keenly feel the push and pull of the tides in their heart. Seablooded orcs are most calm when dwelling near shores or on the open water.

Though all orcs raid human lands during the spring and summer months, this kin is especially feared on the oceans. They are famous pirates, rarely actually coming to shore for raids or skirmishes. It’s said that more than a few merfolk have taken seablooded spouses.

### Seablooded orc talent: Poison Blood

Your black blood is a deadly poison. When this talent is Wounded by a bite, the attacker suffers Critical damage (Piercing and Critical damage).

### Stormblooded

White-skinned like a cloudy sky, these orcs are tumultuously passionate. When great storms blow up off of the ocean, they can hear their own hearts singing to them. They’re most calm when the winds and rains howl.

This kin’s ancestral homeland is the most northerly of all orcish territories. The stormbloods endure the most brutal winters and severe blizzards. They claim these hardships have made them the toughest of the orc broods. Indeed, the stormbloods are nothing if not long-suffering, resourceful, and enduring.

### Stormblooded orc talent: Blur

Your blood smokes like a thick mist. When this talent is Wounded, you become Shrouded. This lasts long enough for you to perform a single action or indefinitely if you stay still and take no actions.

### Fireblooded

Fireblooded orcs bear dark red and black skin that’s warm to the touch. They are never calm.

Firebloods are famously effective as shock troopers. **Orc** clans of other kins will sometimes bring a contingent of firebloods to be used in this way. For this reason, you might find fireblooded mercenaries attached to orcs of all stripes. When the firebloods go berserk, they can punch a hole into the shield-wall of even well-trained and veteran soldiers.

### Fireblooded orc talent: Berserkergang

Your blood is boiling hot. When this talent is Wounded, you may choose to enter a berserker rage. While berserk during a Challenge, you cannot Avoid, Dodge, Speak Incantations, Banter, or Aid Another; however, all of your Attacks are made with favor.

Your rage ends when you defeat every enemy on the field. If an ally has attacked or hurt you during this Challenge, they count as an enemy. You must spend a Resolve to end your rage prematurely.

### Arête

Orcs gain arête by performing the following deeds:

- Hoarding a skull from a class of monster your guild has never killed before

- Hoarding a treasure of great worth

- Slaying a monster at least twice your size

When an orc accomplishes all three arête triggers, they gain the following talent (regardless of kin):

### Orc arête talent: Jarl

You may hatch or gather a horde of goblins to your cause. Goblins are pretty independent little creatures. They see you as “da boss” and take commands from you, but follow those commands in their own, strange, simple little ways.

Assembling a goblin horde is a City Action. Spend any amount of XP to attract 2 + X goblins, where X equals the amount of XP you spent on this action. You may only ever have up to 8 goblins in your horde.

A goblin horde counts as an animal companion. No matter how many goblins are in the horde, they always count as “one creature” and move around together. Goblins understand whatever language you speak, but can only follow one-word commands during Challenges (given using the Command action). They have tiny minds.

Every time a goblin horde takes a Wound, one of its members is killed.

A goblin horde carries or hunts for their own food and supplies their own gear. Their gear is crap; they do not have any items or tools that you can use. They can act as porters: For each goblin in the horde, they can carry one slot worth of items.

### Orcish role-playing concepts

- Orcs are basically metalheads. If it looks like it’s part of the metal subculture, orcs would be into it. Guttural screams, mosh pits, big spikey bracelets, long hair headbanging—orcs have it all.

- Orcs are brutal pillagers and savage pirates, merciless in battle.

- Orcs are also family-oriented, honor-driven, poetic, loyal, and generally well-educated.

- Orcs think a lot about fate. Orcs think that you make your own luck by doing either good or evil actions. Once you've made your choice, nothing can stop destiny from catching up with you.

- Orcs propitiate Rng, god of chaos, in order to avoid their unlucky aid. They perform a dozen or more minor taboos or rituals throughout the day to try and avoid their wrath, such as throwing beads in moving water, making a sign to avert his gaze when they voice a desire, and ceremonially offering them a portion of their meal.

- Orcs think that raiding is good, but stealing is bad. Sneaking into somebody's house and taking their gold is cowardly. Kicking in their front door, putting them to the sword, taking the gold, and setting the house on fire is good.

- Orcs maintain long oral histories. They respect poets and bards as keepers of laws and traditions. These people are unlucky to kill.

- Orcs think that magic is a woman's purview. Witchwomen are unlucky to kill. It is unlucky for a man to do magic.

title: The Four Paths
body:
“Battle not with monsters, lest ye become a monster, And if you gaze into the abyss, the abyss gazes also into you.”

*– Beyond Good and Evil, Friedrich Nietzsche*

Here is a riddle. A fool stands between four kings. The fool bears a long and jagged sword. The kings are unarmed.

The King of Wands speaks first. He is a wicked and powerful sorcerer.

“**If** you slay these others, I will cast a spell that will bind the heart of the most beautiful woman in the world to you. She will be your bride, and by my arts, you will bear many children.”

The King of Cups speaks next. He is a pious man.

“I am advanced in the initiations of Mythrys and speak with the true voice of the Monad. Slay these others, and I will teach you deep wisdom.”

The King of Pentacles then speaks. He is a subtle man and very rich.

“Feh. Pah! Bleh. I have enough gold to buy a woman and the Cult’s favor. Enough of this prattle. Run these other beggars through and you shall have as much gold as you can spend in your lifetime.”

Last speaks the King of Swords—dullest and strongest of the four.

“How is this still being contested? Thou hast a sword. Use it! If thou use it in my name, I shall make thee a knight. All these aforementioned shall be thy reward.”

What does the fool do?

title: Path of Swords
body:
The initial forays into the Underworld were grisly affairs. It was plaster miners who discovered the passage into the first level. They curiously chiseled their way into the antechambers. Like tomb robbers, they discovered gilded treasures and heaps of ancient coins piled therein. And then they discovered the grue. There were no survivors. Before the First Crusade was finally mobilized, the death toll rose terribly as the lure of the Underworld proved irresistible to the very brave and the very foolish. As more of the Underworld began to be revealed, more creatures slithered out of half-remembered legends into reality. Strange beasts and malevolent entities crawled up out of the opened chambers and into the terrorized City. The Cult, at first overwhelmed with the practical considerations and theological questions the Underworld posed, united the proud and ancient houses of mankind with fiery speeches. Under the Cult’s leadership, the First Crusade hunted the monsters that had escaped into the City and encamped themselves on the threshold of the Underworld, warding the lands of men from further attacks. It was only during the Second Crusade that it was discovered that those who die in the Underworld do not stay dead...

### Common motifs:

would-be knight, deposed king, charming pirate, retired gladiator, fanatic vampire hunter, barbarian warrior poet

title: Swords talents
body:
### Aegis

If you are carrying an intact shield and would suffer an effect from a physical source (an attack, a trap, etc.), you may elect to **Notch your shield instead of taking the effect**.

### Doom Eye

When wielding a missile weapon during a Challenge, you may **spend a Sword card on your turn to perform** a **perfect shot**. This Attack automatically hits, regardless of the target’s Initiative.

### Heavy Metal Machine

During Challenges, if you are wearing iron or steel armor, you may use a **miscellaneous action** (discarding any card) to add your **Swords to your Initiative** as an **interrupt** against a single action. You may only use this talent once per round.

### Monster Hunter

When you master or train this talent, choose both a hated foe and a specialization of that enemy.

- You gain a **motif** called “[Foe] Hunter.” You can use this motif to bid lore about these creatures or to gain favor in tests of fate related to them, as normal.

- You make Attacks with favor against foes of your specialization.

Choose a foe and a specialization from the following list—you can change your foe as a City Action if some new type of creature really gives you reason to be pissed off.

### Beast Hunter

You specialize in hunting, tracking, and trapping beasts of all shapes and sizes. What qualifies as a “beast”? Well, if it’s in a medieval bestiary, it’s probably a beast. Beasts are native to the realm of Flesh—they feast, fight, flee, and fuck.

**Specializations:** Any specific species (e.g., bats, centipedes, chimeras, cockatrices, dinosaurs, tigers)

### Elemental Hunter

Your focus is dealing with supernatural embodiments of nature.

**Specializations:** Any specific creature (e.g., undine, salamander, siren, dryad, tree giants)

### Man Hunter

You specialize in the most dangerous game. The term “man” is a bit of a misnomer. This category covers all kith, kin, and genders.

**Specializations:** Any specific kith: fay, humans, underfolk, orcs

### Spirit Hunter

Your focus is on alien intelligences from the far realms. You can deal with incorporeal spirits, manifested spirits, and possessing spirits.

**Specializations:** Spirits from one of the far realms (i.e., Wastes, Weald, Weird, Welkin)

### Undead Hunter

You have experience pacifying the unquiet dead.

**Specializations:** A specific undead type (e.g., skeleton, zombie, wraith)

### Witch Hunter

If the answer to the question “what is that thing?” is “a wizard did it,” you can deal with it.

**Specializations:** Any specific type of magical manifestation (e.g., beastmen, golems, oozes)

### GM’s note

It’s possible that the Monster Hunter categories can overlap. For example, a giant beetle might be a specialty for both a beast hunter and a witch hunter. That’s fine. There’s no reason to get into taxonomical minutiae.

### Reaver

When you Attack during Challenges, you may also move one zone (Set the scene) as **you charge towards your foe**.

### Two-handed Focus

If you are wielding a melee weapon with both hands during a Challenge, you may Attack as a minor action with *either* a Pentacles or a Swords card.

### War Stories

As a Camp Action, tell your guild the story of some of your past adventures. Maybe this was an adventure you've played out in-character, or maybe one in your backstory. You—and everyone who listens and role-plays with you a little— **gets to choose one of the following benefits:**

- **They may charge an uncharged Bond**.

- They gain an extra point of Resolve; this can bring their Resolve up to 5.

### A reminder

During adventurer creation, you will prioritize your attributes—Swords, Pentacles, Cups, or Wands—from 1-4. Whichever attribute is rated 4, the highest rating possible, becomes your path.

Your path determines the initial talents that you have access to. You will begin the game with one of your path’s talents mastered and the rest of your path’s talents in training. More information on learning, training, and mastering talents can be found in chapter 2.

title: Path of Pentacles
body:
Treasure was, and remains, a powerful motivator for Underworld expeditions. The spires of the Castle of Crossed Destinies were literally covered in gold plating until explorers stripped them and hauled the plates back to the surface. The Underworld denizens possess strange coinage as well: round pieces of gold stamped with the faces of three beautiful women and a pentacle star on the reverse. Who these ancient sovereigns were is a matter of great scholarly debate and fanciful public speculation. By the same token, treasure is the primary motivator for the City’s current system of adventuring guilds. The fifty percent guild tax on recovered loot is a heavy burden for adventurers and is much bemoaned. The tax collectors posted at each known exit from the Underworld are a particularly hated lot, but the City has grown rich from this system. Of course, these heavy taxes have created a sprawling industry of smuggling, bribery, and fencing. In pursuit of both relic hunting and black marketeering, “thief” has become a particularly common profession.

### Common motifs:

arrogant duelist, feral scavenger, morbid jester, bounty hunter, traitorous spy, urchin pickpocket, penitent assassin

title: Pentacles talents
body:
### Acrobat

You no longer need to test fate to **climb sheer surfaces** or walk across narrow ledges or tightropes. You climb and scamper along difficult or vertical terrain as easily as walking. During Challenges, you may move this way as a miscellaneous action, as easily as walking to a new zone.

Additionally, if you are prepared, you may **treat a fall** as if it **were** 20’ **shorter** (Falling). If you are not prepared for a fall, you may spend a Resolve to treat it as if it were 20’ shorter.

### Ambusher

In the **first round** of a Challenge, whenever you would deal damage, you **deal 2 Wounds** instead of 1.

Spend a Resolve to resist being ambushed. You raise a hue and cry to warn your guild of the threat beforehand.

### Con Artist

If you spend a few minutes observing a person in conversation or talking to them, you may **bid lore** to ask the GM to **reveal** either one of their **likes** or their **dislikes** (your choice); see Social Encounters & Disposition for more on Disposition and see Creating interesting characters for more about likes and dislikes.

### Fight Dirty

During Challenges, you may Roughhouse as a **minor action** with *either* a **Pentacles or Swords card**. Additionally, you gain several **new Roughhouse options:**

- Exhaust
- Notch
- Silence

### Quick!

During Challenges, if you are wearing light or no armor, you may **treat Pentacles actions as interrupts**.

### Sneak

At any point, you may declare that you go **sneaking**. This allows you to go dramatically off-stage.

Later, if you are not present in a scene and it’s at least somewhat plausible that you could have snuck there, spend a Resolve to arrive on the scene dramatically. If a Challenge has yet to begin, this arrival counts as an ambush (Ambushes and surprise). If combat has already begun, nobody is surprised because everybody is on edge—simply join the flow of combat per usual.

If you go sneaking and all tension evaporates, you may rejoin the scene by slinking out of the shadows. This does not cost a Resolve.

This talent also gives you a new Camp Action: **Infiltrate**. When you Infiltrate, you investigate a specific location that you know of in your current dungeon level. Thereafter, you may bid lore to ask the GM a specific yes or no question about something you’d know having infiltrated that location, e.g., “Is this door trapped?”, “Is this room guarded?”, “Is the wizard’s bedroom on this level?”, “Do the bandits have bows?”, “Were the orcs green-skinned?”

### Up My Sleeve

You may declare that you have had a common, one-slot item with you the whole time. Twice per Crawl (one for each sleeve), spend a **Resolve and declare that you had** a [blank] up your sleeve. This can include a lockpick, a dagger, a handkerchief, an empty vial, a length of wire, or anything else that the GM generally finds viable.

### Sneak responsibly

Be aware of whether or not other adventurers actually want you present in a scene. A heroic rescue out of a prison cell can be much more welcome than you intruding on a personal scene. A player having a solo scene has the right to veto your use of this skill.

title: Path of Cups
body:
When the Underworld opened, so many went on the quest for the Grail of Mythrys that a massive support system, both secular and religious, was assembled. Inns and public houses for the housing of pilgrims, coin changers for foreigners, shops of supply and purveyance, smithies for armament, chapels and shrines for the devout, charlatans and peddlers selling false maps and rumors, scribes and lawyers for drafting of charters and wills, apothecaries for the healing of those returned unsuccessful *—all these sprang up almost overnight. The sign of the Cup has become synonymous for these tradesmen, as well as having a holy connotation, and is still used today to advertise needful service.*

### Common motifs:

grisly apothecary, adventurous cartographer, jolly cleric, daring archaeologist, jaded barber surgeon, young insect tamer

title: Cups talents
body:
### Alchemy

This talent gives you a new Camp Action: **Brew Alchemy**. When you Brew Alchemy, you use an alchemy kit to turn any number of **reagents** you have into **alchemical substances**. Reagents are harvested from the bodies of **Underworld** monsters. Alchemical substances are kept in hermetic bottles and divided into three categories: **potions**, oils, and **bombs**. See Appendix B for more information on alchemy.

### Beast Master

This talent allows you to train and issue commands to your animal companions. As a Camp Action, you may **teach one animal companion one command**. Normal trained animals may learn up to three **commands**. It is possible to retrain an animal with a new command, replacing one of their previously mastered commands.

Pick from this list of commands (or new ones that the GM approves):

- Sic ‘Em
- Hunt
- Get Help
- Do a Trick
- Heel
- Guard
- Fetch
- Stay
- Track

If you have mastered this talent, one animal you own is considered your **familiar**. Familiars can learn **five different commands**. Furthermore, if your familiar would take a Wound that would kill them, you may spend a Resolve to declare that they’re only at Death’s Door and not actually dead.

More information about animal companions can be found in War pigs.

### Bookworm

You have an almost encyclopedic knowledge of everything you have read. Once you have used the Read a Book Camp Action (Camp Actions), you may thereafter **bid lore** to **ask a question about the subject of that text**. Keep a list of books that you’ve read. These are treated like motifs for the purpose of bidding lore, but don’t aid you in tests of fate.

### Chirurgeon

You may provide healing to your companions. You can **expend a poultice to Heal someone** (Effects). This effect cannot be used to clear the Stressed condition.

Additionally, this talent gives you a new Camp Action: **Chirurgery**. When you use Chirurgery on a non-Stressed guild-mate using the Rest and Recover Camp Action, you may Heal all of their Wounds.

### Loremaster

You are a student of ancient languages and lore. This talent confers three advantages:

- You have knowledge of many languages and tongues. You are assumed to be passingly fluent in any spoken language that you might encounter.

- You can translate ancient scripts and runes. Translating a short ancient runic passage that you encounter while delving takes a watch or two. Translating a longer text (such as a book) requires a City Action.

- When you bid lore, you may spend a Resolve instead of spending a lore bid.

title: Counsel
body:
Any time during a Challenge, you may **yell advice** to another adventurer and **hand the player a card from your hand**. The card’s suit must match the action you counsel them to take. The other player may play that card as long as they use it to take your advice. In all other ways, it is treated as a normal Challenge card (Draw Challenge cards).

If you spend a Resolve when you use this talent, the other player may play this card as an interrupt. Otherwise, the standard one-card-per-turn rule remains in effect (Take turns).

You may use this talent once per round.

title: High Chant
body: This talent gives you a new Camp Action: **Perform the High Chant**. When you Perform the High Chant, speak at least two stanzas of epic poetry for the table. If you do so, you may select a number of cards from the minor arcana discard pile equal to your Cups. These are called **inspiration cards**. Distribute the cards to other players—you may keep one for yourself. No player can ever have more than one inspiration card. Inspiration cards may be spent as actions during a Challenge. Alternatively, you may spend your inspiration card instead of drawing from the deck when you test fate or push fate. Inspiration cards last until used or until the end of the session, whichever comes first.

title: Path of Wands
body:
The relationship between the City and magic has been long fraught with bloodshed and sorrow. During the Age of the First Empire, sorcery was used as an act of worship towards the Crow-Headed Queen*—*—one of the earliest deified empresses. During the Age of the Republic, sorcery was seen as being fundamentally tied to both monarchists and elves, and it was made illegal. Still, several cabals flourished in secret. The Age of the Republic was marked by the increasing fanaticism of witch hunters as they attempted to root out these hidden sorcerers. A blanket ban on sorcery proved impossible with the advent of the Age of Dungeon. Too many trials and foes in the Underworld were essentially mystical in nature. The practice of sorcery became a necessary evil, and the Cult began to draw up the appropriate pardons and indulgences. Today, those who practice sorcery in the City must be licensed and registered with the crown. Official sorcerers are granted rods of office by the Tower Gnostic and allowed to join guilds in the exploration of the Underworld. Unofficial sorcery is punishable by fines, but is largely unregulated as long as it is not performed in the City itself. Still, the Witch Finder General remains an influential figure within City politics, and his templars have a much grimmer view of unregulated sorcery.

### Common motifs:

court mage, insane astrologer, artisanal wand maker, conniving charlatan, morbid wizard, doomsday cultist

title: Wands talents
body:
### Counter-spell

You can counter the effects of sorcery with an effort of will. There are two applications for this talent:

- You can stop enemy sorcerers from casting spells in battle. During Challenges, if you can perceive a sorcerer casting a spell, you may **spend a Resolve** to **Speak Incantations** as an **interrupt**.

- If your Speak Incantations value is greater than the enemy sorcerer’s total value, their spell fizzles out.

- If your Speak Incantations value is equal to or less than the enemy’s total value, the spell fizzles out but you must **draw** on the maleficence table as the magic goes awry.

- You can negate a spell already in play. You may spend a Resolve to immediately end the ongoing effects of a spell.

### Dwimmercraft

Suffused with the arcane arts, you can perform small (but meaningful) expressions of magic. You may perform the following **minor effects:**

- You may levitate an object in your zone that weighs about 10 lbs. and that fits comfortably in one hand. You have no fine motor control over this effect, but can bring things to you, lift them up, or push them away.

- You may conjure a showy, harmless, and obviously magical illusion—a shower of sparks, a colorful rainbow stretched between your hands, a flickering image of your first love.

- You conjure a simple illusion of something that you can hold in one hand. Anybody that tries to interact with this object will realize it’s an illusion, but the sight of it is fairly convincing.

Additionally, by spending a Resolve, you can focus your **second sight** for a watch. Second sight allows you to see invisible and Shrouded things. You can perceive the true form of any illusion. You can automatically tell when things are magical or under enchantment. You can also tell if somebody else is a sorcerer.

Using this talent during a Challenge counts as a miscellaneous action.

### Sorcery

Those who walk the Path of Wands are sorcerers. Casting spells and the practice of sorcery is described in detail in **Appendix A: Sorcery**.

### Gramarye

You have learned how to draw on the energies of the far realms. Using this talent, you can release a blast of magical energy up to one zone away through an **archwood wand**, doing damage as a weapon. **During** Challenges, Attacks with your wand count as Wands actions.

Additionally, you gain a new Camp Action: **Make a Pact**. When you Make a Pact, choose to observe one or more pacts from the facing page.

### Magic of the Wastes

You may cast spells of the Wastes. The Wastes are a grim place of death and decay. Spells of this realm deal with matters of undeath, spread fear, or cause harm.

### Magic of the Weald

You may cast spells of the Weald. The Weald is a verdant and wild place. Spells of this realm affect the elements, command beasts, and reshape the natural world.

### Magic of the Weird

You may cast spells of the Weird. The Weird is a place of dream, untouched by sanity. Spells of this realm affect one’s mind and emotions, conjure illusions, and bend reality.

### Magic of the Welkin

You may cast spells of the Welkin. The Welkin is a bright and holy place. Spells of this realm deal with angels, provide healing and protection, and invoke an awful wonder.

title: Pacts
body:
When you use the Make a Pact Camp Action, charge one spell **component** of your choice for each pact made. This charge may be spent in lieu of spending a Resolve to cast the spell, though additional Resolve must still be spent to grant the spell increased power.

Each component may be charged only once. Your pact lasts until broken or until the spell is cast. Components remain charged until the spell is cast or until you break the pact. If you break the pact, draw on the maleficence table.

### Devour the living

You may only eat creatures that are yet living when they pass your lips: maggots, shrimp, mice, infants. If you did not bring these creatures (which are hard to carry and keep), you can test fate with Cups as a Camp Action to see if you can find any in the **Underworld**. If you fail, you are treated as starving (Break bread). If you succeed, you find enough vermin to keep yourself fed comfortably.

### Forego armor

You may not wear armor or helm or wield a shield of any kind, regardless of its construction.

### Forego skins

You may not wear the skins or furs of a beast, or anything derived from them (such as leather). You may wear woven garments of linen or cotton.

### Forego weapons

You may not touch, handle, manipulate, or wield weapons of any kind—not even a rolling pin used as a club. Any weapons you own must be bound in cloth and lashed to your pack. Wands, curiously, do not count as weapons.

### Forego wood

You may not wield, touch, or carry anything made of felled wood. You may not carry a torch, shield, or club. You cannot enjoy the benefits of a fire if that wood was bought with gold in the City (for that wood was certainly felled)—instead, you must sit outside of the fire’s light and heat. Wands, since they’re made of willing archwood, do not count towards this prohibition.

### Gluttony

You must eat more than your share. You must eat double your normal portion (two rations instead of one) whenever you consume rations or this pact is broken.

### Hide your face

You must hide your face behind a mask at all times. Sorcerers might choose masks of porcelain, cloth, wood, bone, or more exotic materials. Wearing a mask incurs disfavor on all social tests, and the GM will accommodate your social encounters accordingly.

### Self-mortification

You must purchase and wear a hair shirt under your normal clothing. This causes you to be Stressed. If you take off the hair shirt and clear Stressed, you violate this pact.

### Self-mutilation

When you make this pact, you cut runes into yourself. This causes you to take a Wound. If you ever heal this Wound, you violate this pact.

### Silence

If you must speak, you must speak in a whisper. People must be very close to you and it must be very quiet to hear your words. If you speak in a loud voice, you violate this pact.

### Verity

You must not tell a knowing lie. If you do so, even in jest, this pact is broken.

### Damned if you do, damned if you don’t…

Sometimes, pacts might put you in situations where you have to break one pact to keep another. This has its roots in mythology. Consider how Cú Chulainn couldn’t refuse food from a stranger, nor could he eat dog meat. When a stranger offers him dog meat, he’s on the hook one way or another. We recommend not shying away from these conflicts. If the fiction in your game demands that two pacts contradict each other, fine. It’s ultimately not that painful. Let it play out and see what happens.

title: The Crawl Phase
body:
“There’s a great maze of tunnels, a Labyrinth. It’s like a great dark city, under the hill. Full of gold, and the swords of old heroes, and old crowns, and bones, and years, and silence.”

*– The Tombs of Atuan, Ursula K. Le Guin*

There are strange things the rumor of which the sun has never heard. Between sprawls of empty space in the Underworld, there is weirdness.

There are orreries that presage the position of alien moons un-glimpsed by the eye of man.

There are colonies of lost adventurers driven mad, endlessly critiquing the architecture of the Inverted Castle.

There are hallways filled with gnashing teeth.

There are fields of dragon bones that roar whenever an orc walks among them.

There are three wells, reflecting scenes of the past, the present, and the future.

There are exiled stars seeking to marry off their daughters with the dowry of a wish.

There are fungi gardens watered by the tears of nymphs.

And what is in the center of the maze?

title: The Flow of the Crawl Phase
body:
A new game of *His Majesty the Worm* starts at the gates to the Underworld. The Crawl begins with the guild taking their first steps into those lightless depths.

### The mythic underworld

*His Majesty the Worm’s* setting is a place described in fiction, folklore, and games as a mythic underworld. A mythic underworld is not merely a cave system with kobolds and goblins hiding in every shadowy corner. It is another world, charged with unconventional physics, inhuman entities, and alien architectures.

The Crawl is the phase of the game centered on exploring the Underworld. When the guild leaves the safety of civilization to pursue their quests, negotiating with strange creatures, avoiding traps, and excavating ancient treasures, they are Crawling. Most of the game is focused on this phase.

The Underworld is what is called a **megadungeon**. A megadungeon is inherently strange. It does not need to conform to the players’ conceptions and expectations. It does benefit from having internal logic, however. Learning the “rules” of the Underworld is fun, and having internally consistent logic allows players to make meaningful choices (which is the point of the game).

A megadungeon is composed of smaller, constituent **dungeons**. Each dungeon is a thematic level, section, or subsection. For example, your Underworld might be composed of five dungeon levels, which are called the Spires, the Castle of Crossed Destinies, the Inverted Castle, the City of Ruin, and the Necropolis of Ot.

### Characteristics of a mythic underworld

1. It’s big, and has many levels; in fact, it may be endless 2. It follows its own ecological and physical rules 3. It is not static; the inhabitants and even the layout may grow or change over time 4. It is not linear 5. There are many ways to move up and down through the levels 6. Its purpose is mysterious or shrouded in legend 7. It’s inimical to those exploring it 8. Deeper or farther levels are more dangerous 9. It’s a (the?) central feature of the campaign

– “The Dungeon as a Mythic Underworld,” Philotomy’s Musings

Dungeons are separated into different **rooms**. A room can be any discrete space: a chamber, a feasting hall, a natural cavern, an underground river, etc. Each room should have something interesting for the players to interact with. For example, one room in the Castle of Crossed Destinies could have a giant throne constructed of a titan’s bones, another room could be the lair of a reverse sphinx who needs to hear riddles to survive, and so on.

As the guild explores each room, random events called the Meatgrinder create tension. The Meatgrinder represents the passage of time: torches burning low, patrolling monsters, and other hazards.

**Each dungeon level has both a map and a Meatgrinder table, both full of interesting things to discover.** When players travel into a new room, the GM looks at the room description. Simultaneously, the GM draws a random card from the major arcana and consults the Meatgrinder table. They then describe the newly-entered room in the context of the random Meatgrinder encounter.

This chapter details what players need to know about the Crawl Phase. Advice for the GM for running the Crawl Phase is found in chapter 10. Procedures for the GM to create the Underworld are found in Appendix E: Underworld Creation.

Play happens through a combination of what the GM describes and the decisions the players make. It’s not a preplanned story.

During the Crawl, the players tell the GM where they want to go. They use an in-character map to make sure everybody is on the same page about where the guild currently is.

The GM describes what the guild encounters as they travel. The GM describes the contents of each room within the context of a random Meatgrinder event.

When the guild encounters dangers—crushing walls, minotaurs, anti-life fields, swindling merchants—the players and the GM engage in a dialogue.

- The GM describes the situation, the players ask questions about the scene, and the GM clarifies.

- The players describe what their adventurers attempt, the GM asks questions about their actions and their intentions, and the players clarify.

- The GM describes what happens as a result of the adventurer’s actions. If there’s risk or doubt about the adventurer’s ability to accomplish their goals, the GM calls for a test of fate (Tests of Fate).

“Folk like to pretend they know everything about the world. [...] You don’t have blanks on your map, so the folks who draw them shade in a piece and write, ‘The Eld.’ You might as well burn a hole right through the map for what good that does.”

*– The Wise Man’s Fear, Patrick Rothfuss*

### The rumor mill

A large part of *His Majesty the Worm* is exploring and discovering. If one (or, gods forbid, all) of a guild’s adventurers die, it’s boring to rediscover and retread old ground. That’s why we have a rule called the **rumor mill**.

Adventurers are always talking in taverns about what they’ve discovered, what they’ve fought, and what’s almost eaten them whole. Unless the adventurers make an effort to keep something about their delvings secret, assume that it’s generally common knowledge. Therefore, adventurers who are introduced later into the game’s story can know things that previous adventurers discovered. They know where the secret switches are, they know how to defeat Mother Maggot, they know how to safely cross the invisible bridge.

Despite the presence of otherworldly and strange beings, very few creatures attack on sight and fight to the death. (Well, perhaps skeletons. They want to free their boney brethren from the flesh prisons that you’re cruelly keeping them in.) Almost everything can be talked to, negotiated with, or at least avoided. See “Disposition” see Social Encounters & Disposition for an overview of negotiating with the GM’s characters.

When combat cannot be avoided, the Crawl Phase transitions into the Challenge Phase. Once the Challenge is resolved, the Challenge Phase transitions back to the Crawl.

Mysteriously, the Underworld has a property that preserves life. When a mortal blow is dealt, the victim lingers at Death’s Door before dying. This property has prolonged the life of many adventurers who have run afoul of the Underworld’s treachery.

Those who *do* die in the Underworld rise again as undead…

title: Abandon All Hope, Ye Who Enter Here
body:
As you explore, you will find hazards that need to be navigated around, avoided, or retreated from.

This is a game about interacting with the world as if it actually exists. Because RPGs are conversation games, you explore the game world through asking questions. You can ask what your adventurer can see, feel, hear, etc. No need to draw cards—just ask what you can perceive and the GM will answer you honestly. As the GM describes things, follow up with specific questions to dig deeper into the game world.

There’s no list of skills or abilities to limit what you can do within the fictional world. Don’t ask “Can I make some sort of test to look for…” or “Can I make a test to disarm…” Instead ask questions like “Is there any tension as I slowly open the door?” or “Do I hear anything if I tap on the wall here?” Interrogate your surroundings by asking questions and state your character’s actions: the GM will tell you if you need to make a test of fate.

That said, your character sheet might contain something you can use to your advantage! You might have an item, spell, or talent that you can put to a clever use. Your success and your failure are defined by your ideas.

### Locked doors

Some doors are locked.

If the door has a keyhole, you might find the key in the pockets of a dungeon denizen on this level. Keys tend to be coded: the copper key fits in the copper door, the mermaid-shaped key fits in the door painted with mermaids, etc.

If the door has a keyhole, you can also try to pick the lock with lockpicks. Picking a lock with lockpicks requires a successful test of Pentacles.

You can also try to force a door. You might bash it down with a test of Swords. A tool like a battering ram or crowbar provides favor to this test.

Some doors can only be opened by a particular mechanism. You need to say a particular pass phrase, twist the taxidermied moose head, depress all four pressure plates in the room, etc. If a door seems stuck, come back to it later. You might have more perspective on how to open it after exploring further. Ask dungeon denizens if they have any advice.

### Secret doors

Some doors are secret. These doors might be obscured (behind a bookshelf ) or built to be all but invisible (stone doors that only open when you twist a candle sconce).

You find secret doors by describing how you search for them. You can look at a wall to see if you can see any seams. You can tap on a wall to hear if it sounds hollow. You can look behind curtains, inside wardrobes, and under rugs to see if there’s anything there.

Look at your map. Are there any gaps where a room would logically make sense? Look for secret doors there.

Look for patterns. Secret doors are hidden in places that make sense for them to be. If you find a secret door behind one portrait, search behind other portraits to see if there’s a pattern to be found.

If you don’t ask for specific information and simply say, “I spend as long as it takes to search the room for hidden doors,” the GM can use the “Moving carefully” rules. They tell you if there’s a secret door but draw on the Meatgrinder to see if your torches gutter due to the time you take searching.

### Checking for traps

Some doors, rooms, or passageways are trapped. You find traps by describing how you search for them.

Open the door very slowly to feel if there’s a trigger in the hinges that activates a trap. Bend down and check to see if there’s a tripwire in the door frame. Walk carefully to check if there are any pressure plates in the hallway.

If you create a procedure like “We walk down the hallway tapping the floor in front of us with our ten-foot pole,” the GM can use the “Moving carefully” rules due to the time involved in the search. They tell you if you find any traps but draw on the Meatgrinder to see if your torches gutter due to the time you take searching.

### Dealing with traps

Some traps might be unavoidable no matter how carefully you search. You decide how to deal with the traps you trigger.

Some traps will simply occur—the room begins to fill with water as soon as the door is opened. Other traps allow you to make a test of fate to avoid the worst outcome—you test Pentacles to grasp the edge of the collapsing bridge as it falls apart.

The way you describe your actions when a trap is triggered will determine how the GM adjudicates what happens next.

Here are some examples.

### Example the first

As the guild steps into a room, the door slams shut and locks. With a grinding sound, the east and west walls slowly begin moving towards each other, threatening to crush all within like a giant trash compactor.

*What do you do?*

Some suggestions:

- Was a guild member trapped outside when the door slammed shut? Are there controls anywhere they can use to deactivate the trap?

- Do you have pitons in your pack? Can you drive them into the wall to slow or stop the walls’ advance?

- Is the door flush with the wall? Is there any space in the door frame in which to hide yourself?

- Can you search for a secret door? Is there a service panel on the walls? In the ceiling? On the floor?

- Do you have a crowbar? Can you pry open the door?

- Is there a troll in your party? Do they have the Colossal talent? Can they smash down the door or break the mechanism behind the walls through sheer strength?

- Do you have a slime bomb? Can you throw it to Destroy part of the wall or the door?

- Do you have the Portable Hole spell? Can you cast it on the wall to see the mechanism beyond? Can you jam or disrupt the mechanism if you reach your hand through the hole?

### Example the second

You find a door set into a frame resembling the face of a green devil. Inside the green devil’s mouth is a black hole. It’s not just dark, a literal void exists within the green devil’s mouth.

*What do you do?*

Some suggestions:

- Discretion is the better part of valor. If you don’t need to deal with the green devil face, can you simply leave?

- If you need to deal with the face, are there any switches or buttons hidden? Can you press the eyes? Can you twist the horns?

- Don’t interact with the void in the mouth with your bare hands. Throw a sling stone into it. Touch it with a staff at a distance.

- Does someone in your guild have the Counter-spell talent? Does it have any effect on the face?

### Example the third

As you walk down the hall, you step on a pressure plate. You hear a “CLICK!” as it sinks into the floor. You hear mechanisms whirring in the walls, like a machine spinning up.

With a split-second decision to make, you don’t have a lot of information to act on—but doing something is better than nothing.

*What do you do?*

Some suggestions:

- Can you keep pressure on the pressure plate in case releasing it is the trap’s trigger?

- Can you drop prone to try and avoid whatever is coming? Can you do so while depressing the plate?

- Do you have a shield? Can you bring it to bear to protect yourself from potential threats?

- Does somebody in your guild have the Aegis talent? Can they use it for your benefit if the trap is sprung?

title: Maps
body:
Before the game, the GM will map out the Underworld and create detailed notes about each room’s contents. They will also create a basic map for each dungeon level for the players: **this is your guild’s in-character map**.

Your map lets you tell the GM where your guild wants to go. For example, you might say, “We’re going to head towards Room 202.” Because the room numbers will be the same between the GM’s notes and the player’s map, the GM can turn to their description for Room 202 and continue play with minimal page flipping.

The player-facing map does not contain any information about the contents of dungeon rooms. However, each map should:

- Show the basic outline of the rooms;

- Show the paths through the dungeon; and

- Be keyed, with each room having a different number.

Although you’re given some information on the map, it might not be complete! As you travel, you might find hidden rooms that you can draw directly onto your map. Exploring and discovering secrets is the fun part of play!

As you fill your (mostly) blank map in with notes about the rooms, traps, and dungeon denizens you encounter, you’ll be able to make informed decisions as you explore.

title: Watches
body:
Travel time is measured in **watches**. A watch isn't a concrete period of time; it might be an hour or ten minutes or all night. It’s hard to tell how much time is *actually* passing in the Underworld. Time moves weirdly—happy moments burn away quickly, whereas tense moments stretch like lengthening shadows. Watches are just a way to talk about how quickly, quietly, and carefully you're moving.

A watch passes:

- Each time the guild passes into a new room on the map;

- Whenever the guild spends a long time performing a task (such as taking a door off of its hinges, repairing a broken machine, counting the jelly beans in a jar); and

- Each Camp and Challenge Phase.

When a watch passes, the GM draws a card from the major arcana deck and compares the result to the Meatgrinder table for that dungeon. The GM then describes the Meatgrinder event in the context of the new or current scene.

title: Meatgrinder
body:
The Meatgrinder is a collection of impermanent events—things like monster patrols, weather, or bumping into a rival guild. Importantly, the rate at which your light sources **flicker** and go out is controlled by the Meatgrinder; see Light for more information on light sources.

As you travel, the GM will describe scenes that combine the contents of each room and the results of the Meatgrinder. For example, if the room you enter is a dragon’s lair and the GM randomly pulls a patrol of goblins from the Meatgrinder table, you might find goblins attempting to sneak into the dragon’s lair for treasure—and making entirely too much noise in the process.

When a Meatgrinder event is triggered, the GM should mark it off. If the cards are shuffled and the GM draws the same event twice, nothing happens and the guild has a watch of respite. The GM repopulates their Meatgrinder tables after each City Phase.

The full procedure to create a Meatgrinder for a dungeon level is detailed in Appendix E, see Create the Meatgrinder. Here are the basics.

In general, Meatgrinder tables follow this formula:

- **Torches gutter (I–V):** *Torches guttering* represents time passing as your light sources grow dim. When torches gutter, all light sources **flicker**.

- Torches gutter events are not marked off from the Meatgrinder. They can occur multiple times.

- **Curiosities (VI–X):** *Curiosities* are moments of serendipity. “Nothing happens” is a boring result for a random table. Curiosities are an opportunity for a GM to interject color into the black depths of the Underworld. They can serve as inspiration for role-playing exchanges or provide hints about the local environment.

- **Travel events (XI–XV):** *Travel events* represent things that go wrong during the journey. They might require you to make a hard choice about resource management or ask you to test fate to avoid a hardship. Travel events might prompt Challenges.

- **Random encounters (XVI–XX):** *Random encounters* are chance meetings with the denizens of the Underworld. These might be friendly encounters with would-be allies, hazardous encounters with hungry animals, or murderous encounters with monsters. Interesting random encounters don’t simply list “monster type.” The best random encounters paint a small scenario that the GM can use as inspiration for a Challenge.

- **Quest rumor (XXI):** *Quest rumors* lead you one step closer to your current quest. Quest rumors provide hints or directions towards your quest goal. If you’ve already made significant progress on your current quest, this result might even feature the object of your quest.

title: Loud Noises
body: Every time the guild makes a loud noise or otherwise draws attention to themselves, the GM should **pull** on the Meatgrinder table. If the draw results in a **random encounter** (results XVI–XX), the GM describes an encounter with the wandering creature drawn to the noise. Otherwise, nothing happens.

title: Moving Carefully
body: If the guild is proceeding very slowly or methodically, tapping in front of them with their ten-foot pole, the GM should **pull** again on the Meatgrinder table after resolving potential encounters. If the second draw results in **torches guttering** (results I–V), the GM keeps the result to represent additional time passing. Otherwise, nothing happens.

title: Example Meatgrinder table
body:
| Card | Meatgrinder Event |
|:---:|---|
| I | Torches gutter |
| II | Torches gutter |
| III | Torches gutter |
| IV | Torches gutter |
| V | Torches gutter |
| VI | [Curiosity] Local Fauna: The guild startles up a flock of luminescent cave butterflies. They flutter away quickly. |
| VII | [Curiosity] Cockatrice Call: The guild hears a cockatrice’s peacock-like shriek, distantly. |
| VIII | [Curiosity] Orcish Graffiti: The guild notices some graffiti in Vetus chalked onto the cavern wall. It reads: “Ulf is no true orc. If he wishes to win my hand in marriage, he must defeat me in combat.” (The GM can accept lore bids on this curiosity as appropriate.) |
| IX | [Curiosity] Blind Fish Pool: The guild wanders by a shallow pool. The water looks clear, but the pool is full of toothy, blind fish. |
| X | [Curiosity] Nearby Flowers: The air is full of a heady floral scent. If the guild searches around a little, they’ll find a bunch of pale blue and purple lilies sprouting nearby. Appropriate lore bids will show that they are normal flowers with few (if any) meaningful alchemical properties, but they are quite lovely and might make a nice bouquet for someone. |
| XI | [Travel event] Droppings: The first person in the marching order accidentally steps in some droppings. If they can’t find a way to get clean soon, they’ll become Stressed. If the guild investigates, they realize that the droppings are from an ogre. It looks no more than a day old. |
| XII | [Travel event] Rushing River: The guild encounters a rushing river which has risen past its banks. It’s impossible to ford without getting soaked. The guild can either turn back and try and find an alternate route or attempt to cross. Swimming across the river requires a test of Swords. If successful, they make it across safely. If the test fails, they suffer a Wound from almost drowning. Whether successful or not, anybody who braved the cold waters becomes Stressed. If no precautions were taken, fragile items in backpacks (scrolls, provisions) are soaked and Destroyed. |
| XIII | [Travel event] Hole in Pack: While traveling, a random adventurer discovers that their pack has a hole in it. The last listed item in their pack has fallen out and disappeared. (Backtracking and performing a thorough search will prompt additional watches to pass.) |
| XIV | [Travel event] Bad Scene: The guild comes upon a field of faintly glowing green mushrooms sporadically sending up little clouds of dust. In the middle of the field is a corpse in rusted armor. A cracked chest lies near the corpse. (It’s all bad news. Mushrooms are poisonous. Corpse is a zombie. Chest? Probably bad too. But there’s also gold in the chest and that’s good.) |
| XV | [Travel event] Webs: The guild’s path forward is blocked by thick layers of web. However, they can see several hanging sacks dangling from the cavern ceiling. Are these other adventurers who met a grim fate? Could they be rescued? |
| XVI | [Random encounter] Red Herring Tavern: The guild happens upon a squat but cozy-looking tavern. A wooden sign depicts a red fish leaping from the water (a herring, if anybody bids lore). Inside is a tapped barrel of ale and a cauldron full of stew, but no innkeeper to be seen. In fact, the tavern is a giant mimic occupied by several smaller mimics. Sleeping in the mimic tavern is a notably bad idea. |
| XVII | [Random encounter] Cockatrice: A cockatrice has taken its chicks out to teach them how to hunt. |
| XVIII | [Random encounter] Ogre Courting Ritual: An amorous ogre is trying to impress a she-ogre with increasingly ridiculous feats of strength. They are both making a terrible racket. |
| XIX | [Random encounter] Orc Hooligans: A gang of three orc youths accompanied by a random number of goblins are on a quest to make a name for themselves before returning to their clan. They might see the guild as an appropriate challenge or be convinced to join with the guild against some greater foe. |
| XX | [Random encounter] Gentle Simon: An owlbear has treed Gentle Simon of Heartsbane, a notoriously shrimpy sorcerer. All of Gentle Simon’s Resolve has been expended trying to rescue himself, and he’s now beginning to weep. |
| XXI | [Quest rumor] Victims of Geralt Mourn: The adventurers find a rival guild crucified. They are still alive, though grievously injured and dehydrated. If the adventurers can provide aid, healing, and food, the rival party gasps about their recent encounter with the vampire Geralt Mourn, who the guild has sworn to slay. It was this dread vampire who crucified them as a warning to others. They have news of his current whereabouts, but would be loath to tangle with him again. |

### What work is the Meatgrinder doing?

The **Meatgrinder** introduces the tension of a ticking clock to your Crawl. If you linger too long or travel too deep, your torches will all burn out and you will be lost in a lightless void.

Also, the alchemical reaction between the random event and the specific room ensures that the scene is interesting for everybody at the table—GM and player alike. A trapped hallway encounter can be fun on its own, but the (randomly generated) inclusion of a rival adventuring party approaching from the opposite direction adds a dynamic element. And, if you ever retrace your steps and enter this hallway again, some other random element will be encountered here. Since you’ve traveled here before, you can leverage what you learned from the first encounter to your advantage in the second.

title: Light
body:
What lurks just outside the halo of your torchlight? In the sunless depths, a candle is the difference between life and death.

There are three levels of lighting while exploring dark places: bright, dim, **and dark**.

### Bright light

If you are holding a light source, you benefit from bright light. Bright light means that you can operate without penalty.

If you’re holding a light source, you’re always clearly visible. Hiding is impossible.

### Dim light

Even a little light offers hope in the darkness. If you aren’t carrying a light source (while someone else in your guild is), you’re considered to be in dim lighting. Any complex or visually-dependent task—such as picking locks, surgery, investigation, crafting—suffers disfavor on tests of fate while you are in dim lighting unless an adventurer with a light source actively provides illumination.

If you are in dim lighting, you may attempt to hide behind cover.

title: Darkness
body:
No matter how accomplished an adventurer is, darkness is crippling. You are Blind while in darkness. Most activities are simply impossible to accomplish in the dark—others may be attempted but **suffer disfavor**.

Crawling in the dark is a futile pursuit. The guild is at risk of every pitfall and every trap, and creatures accustomed to darkness will find them easy prey.

“It is pitch black. You are likely to be eaten by a grue.”

*– Zork, Infocom*

title: Flickers
body:
The Omphalic Market lists candles, torches, and lanterns for purchase. Each type of light source can flicker a certain number of times before it is extinguished.

Your light source **flickers** when the Meatgrinder says **torches gutter**. Candles can flicker 2 times. Torches can flicker 3 times. Lanterns can flicker 4 times.

Candles, torches, and lanterns are not designed for violence. Your light source automatically breaks and is extinguished if:

- It is hit in combat

- You use it as a weapon in combat

You can tie your lantern to your belt, but if you suffer a Wound, your lantern is also Destroyed, covering you in oil.

Dropping your light source might cause it to go out.

- Torches have a 50% chance of staying lit or being extinguished when dropped. Extinguished torches can’t be relit.

- Candles are extinguished when dropped. Candles may be relit.

- Lanterns are Destroyed when dropped.

title: We’re Doomed!
body:
If the guild is *completely* out of light sources, each player draws on the table below.

| Card | Doom |
|:---:|---|
| I–VII | You are eaten by a grue. |
| VIII | You are captured by monsters. The GM chooses an appropriate monster based on the Meatgrinder table. Escaping guild members know your general location and the type of monster. |
| IX | You are held for ransom by the bird-faced Olu Gang. It takes 1,000 gold per guild Fame (Deeds and Fame) to buy your freedom. |
| X | You are lost in the Underworld. The GM places your adventurer as an encounter on the Meatgrinder table. That character may reenter play if you are encountered. Make a new adventurer for the time being. |
| Page | You make it back to the surface, but only after making solemn oaths to forsake the adventuring life. You retire. The GM controls your character in the City. |
| Knight | You scramble back to the surface naked and shivering. You lose all of your equipment, both from your belt and backpack. |
| Queen | You limp back to the surface, shaken to your core. You have a 50% chance to have lost each item carried, tested individually. |
| King | You limp back to the surface, mostly unscathed but raving about the twelve different flavors of darkness. |

title: Stress
body:
### The logic of Stress

Have you ever had a player in a game who insisted their character would happily sit in a dungeon room for twelve hours and just count coins until they found the cursed one? Or that their character would jump into an open sewer to search for the dagger they just dropped? Has the same friend ever turned down a slice of pizza because it had pineapple on it?

The **Stressed** condition does two things. First, it represents the trauma of the human experience in the mythic Underworld. Second, it disincentivizes choices that are on the extremes of human tolerability but have no other mechanical weight.

If a player wants their adventurer to ford the freezing river, they’re welcome to do it. However, such an event would be physically taxing. As such, the GM should warn the player that such an action would cause them to become **Stressed**.

Adventuring is nasty and uncomfortable. When you undergo a traumatic experience or suffer physical distress, check the Stressed condition. In short, when you’re shivering, hungry, or terrified, you are Stressed.

Being Stressed has no immediate negative effects, but it makes recovery during the Camp Phase more taxing. You *must* **clear Stressed before healing any other condition**.

The GM is the ultimate arbiter of what introduces Stress or not. In general, being Stressed is less serious than taking actual physical harm, but makes your adventurer angry, weak, sore, or miserable.

**Example** stressors: exposure to extreme elements without the appropriate gear; magically terrifying monsters like liches or dragons; self-harm; extremely mundane, boring, and repetitive tasks; long-term social isolation; witnessing torture; and so on.

title: Item Durability
body:
Adventuring is hard on both your body and your gear. Items can be Notched or Destroyed while adventuring.

Items might be damaged by environmental hazards. For example, a trap that shoots a jet of fire might Notch any flammable items on your belt. Items can also be damaged as a consequence of your actions. For example, if you throw your net over a charging manticore to help your companion escape, the manticore tears the net to shreds. The GM arbitrates when items are damaged.

### Repairing items

Tinker’s kits can be used during the Camp Phase to repair Notched items (but not Destroyed items). Spending your Camp Action to use a tinker’s kit removes 1 Notch.

Notched and Destroyed items can be repaired if carried back to the City, see Replacing and repairing gear.

Fragile items are Destroyed after 1 Notch. Items intended for durability are Destroyed after 2 Notches. Items made of tempered steel are Destroyed after 3 Notches.

title: Falling
body:
If you fall from a great height, you suffer 1 Piercing Wound (Piercing and Critical damage) for each 10’ you fall (rounded down). For example, if you fall from a 25’ height, you would suffer 2 Wounds that cannot be absorbed with armor.

Whenever you fall, you may test Pentacles.

- If you fail, take damage as normal.

- If you succeed, treat the fall as 10’ shorter. For example, if you fall 25’ and succeed in the test of Pentacles, you only suffer 1 Piercing Wound.

- On a great success, treat the fall as 20’ shorter (e.g., a 25’ fall would do no damage).

- On a great failure, you take damage as normal and any fragile items (like hermetic bottles) on your belt or in your pack are Destroyed.

title: Afflictions
body:
If you’ve drunk tainted water from a huldra’s body-choked well, inhaled a cloud of spores from a creeping mold, or developed an infected cut from a goblin’s shit-covered dagger, you become **afflicted**.

Afflictions—be they poison, disease, infection, addiction, or otherwise—are essentially countdown clocks to doom. Each affliction has a number of stages, each with a specific effect.

- Most afflictions have increasingly negative effects for each stage.

- Some afflictions—notably drugs—have positive effects at their early stages.

- Some afflictions have *death* at their final stage.

When you gain an affliction, you immediately gain its stage 1 effect.

To track your progress with the affliction, **draw** a **circle**. **Draw** as many sections as there are stages of the affliction. Color in the first section with **hatch marks**.

*For example*

**Afflictions automatically progress to the next stage at the end of each Camp Phase**.

title: Curing an affliction
body:
To cure an affliction, take the Rest and Recover action during the Camp Phase (Camp Actions). During this action, you’ll burn charged Bonds. One stage of the affliction is cured after a certain number of charges are spent.

Burned charges are cumulative. For example, if a stage of an affliction is cured for every 3 charges spent, you can burn 1 charge over the course of three Camp Phases to cure a single stage.

The GM determines the number of charges needed to cure a stage of a particular affliction. Players are not told this information up front, but a well-worded lore bid might reveal these details. When Resting and Recovering, you tell the GM how many charges you are burning and hope for the best.

Burned charges cure the most severe stages first, whether or not the affliction has progressed to that point. To represent a cured stage, color a section of the circle in **black**. You will never experience the effects associated with a cured stage. **The affliction** is **completely healed when all** stages **are cured**.

*For example*

Certain things are healthful for curing an affliction:

- Some afflictions have very specific cures (e.g., the poison of a basilisk can be cured by the gallbladder of a basilisk).

- Bezoars and leeches (available at the Omphalic Market, see Bezoar) give charges for healing.

- The Life spell reduces an affliction by an entire stage, perhaps curing it entirely.

Afflictions progress to the next stage at the end of each Camp Phase unless the stage above it has been cured. Essentially, afflictions progress clockwise, but are cured counter-clockwise.

### In summation

- Your affliction begins at stage 1.

- During the Crawl Phase, you have the opportunity to search for healing items or chirurgeons to help your recovery during the Camp Phase.

- During the step 1 of your next Camp Phase, you can Rest and Recover to burn charges in an attempt to recover from the affliction. These charges can come from charged Bonds or healthful items. These charges go towards curing the final stage first (sections are blacked out on the affliction clock in a counterclockwise manner).

- At the end of the Camp Phase, your affliction progresses one stage (clockwise on the affliction clock). If the stage beyond it has already been cured, you remain at your current affliction stage.

- If you cure the stage that you are already on, your affliction regresses by one stage.

title: Example afflictions
body:
Here are some “common” afflictions to use as examples. **GMs** can tweak these to create any manner of gross old disorders for their players.

### Giant rat venom

A green rat the size of a dog, covered in buboes, welts, and goiters, bites you. It only gets worse from there.

**Stage 1:** The wound turns ugly: green and fetid. It begins to stink, but there are no other effects.

Requires 1 charge to cure.

**Stage 2:** You feel like hot garbage. You become permanently Exhausted.

Requires 1 charge to cure.

**Stage 3:** Your lungs are filled with green mucus. Every time you test fate, you take a Piercing Wound after the test is resolved.

Requires 2 charges to cure.

### Ghost lotus

The seeds of the ghost lotus rewrite pathways in the user’s brain. The feeling is incredibly addictive. Habitual users of the lotus (called lotusphages) become very strange and otherworldly: their personalities change, their memories become distorted, and they have trouble distinguishing between the waking world and dreams.

**Stage 1:** You experience euphoria. This effect cancels out any effects that hamper your ability to sleep.

Requires 1XP to recover from stage 1. No charges are otherwise needed.

**Stage 2:** At this stage, you lose the ability to understand representative thought. Paintings and illustrations are just blobs of color. Words are meaningless lines on paper. You cannot read. You cannot write. You are also immune to illusions.

Requires 2 charges to cure.

**Stage 3:** You become lost in a waking dream. Rewrite one of your motif descriptors. For example, if you have the “Romancing Swordsman” motif, replace “Romancing” with another word (e.g., Ambitious, Addled, Drowsy, Sadistic, etc.).

Requires 1 charge to cure.

### The great contagion

“Oh Mythrys, do I have the red welts? I have the red welts don’t I? I’m going to die. Tell Mama I love her.”

**Stage 1:** Your skin breaks out into red whorls that are very painful to the touch. You take a Piercing Wound.

Requires 2 charges to cure.

**Stage 2:** You take Critical damage.

Requires 2 charges to cure.

**Stage 3:** You die.

title: Black Honey
body:
A thick molasses that tastes so, so sweet. It’s like meth and speed had a terrifying demon baby. You act preternaturally fast while on the honey.

Each time you take black honey, you are re-exposed to the affliction. If you’ve previously cured stage 2, erase the marking in the stage 2 section.

**Stage 1:** If you’ve recently taken black honey, you may choose to draw 5 cards during an encounter instead of 4. If you do so, you spit out 1–4 teeth.

Requires 5 charges to quit.

**Stage 2:** You’re jittery and sweaty. Your Cups score equals 1 and you suffer disfavor on all tests of fate that require fine motor control.

Requires 1 charge to calm down to stage 1.

title: Social Encounters & Disposition
body:
In the Underworld, you’ll encounter the bizarre denizens of the dungeons and the adventurers trying their best to slay them (or you).

Role-playing the characters you encounter is one of the GM’s many jobs. The GM is provided with guidelines for role-playing called Disposition. Advice for GMs creating characters with interesting personalities and running social encounters is provided in Creating interesting characters.

Each Disposition has three steps of severity: **mild, basic**, and **intense**. Mild emotions are on the inside of the circle; intense emotions are on the outside of the circle. Related emotions are grouped near each other.

title: Starting Disposition
body:
A character’s starting Disposition informs the GM how that creature should initially act, how hostile or friendly it is to the guild, and what they’re likely to demand in a parlay.

Sometimes a character’s starting Disposition will be obvious based on the scenario in which the guild encounters them. If there is any question, or if randomness is desired, the GM should look at the top card in the discard pile of the minor arcana.

| Card | Disposition |
|:---:|---|
| I–II | Anger |
| III–IV | Distaste |
| V–VI | Sadness |
| VII–VIII | Joy |
| IX–X | Surprise |
| Page–Knight | Trust |
| Queen–King | Fear |

Characters with positive Dispositions (e.g., joy, trust) negotiate in good faith. They will acquiesce to reasonable requests in exchange for a reasonable exchange from the guild. Characters with intense positive Dispositions might even provide extra aid and advice.

Characters with negative Dispositions (e.g., angry, distaste) want to bring the conversation to an end. They don’t have any interest in exchanging goods or services with the guild. If the encounter continues at all, it will be in a combative capacity—transition to the Challenge Phase.

title: Influencing Disposition
body:
As you role-play with a GM character, their Dispositions change based on how your actions interact with their personality. All intelligent creatures can be negotiated with (assuming a shared language). When role-playing with the GM’s characters, you don’t have to speak in a silly voice or use faux Shakespearean language. You don’t even have to say exactly what your character is saying, word for word. You do have to say what you want and how you are approaching the conversation.

- You might flatter the vain countess.

- You might make pious platitudes to the unctuous priest.

- You might offer rare trash to the goblin trash merchant.

These strategies only make sense when applied towards that particular character; offering trash to the vain countess would be unwise.

The GM judges the results of a negotiation based on how what you said aligns or conflicts with their character’s personality. Depending on the outcome of the role-playing exchange, the GM character’s Disposition either increases/decreases in severity or shifts to a related emotion.

- Good ideas and strong bargaining chips that appeal to a character’s likes and wants will automatically create positive Dispositions.

- Approaches that conflict with the character’s dislikes will automatically create negative Dispositions.

- When the situation is risky and there’s something at stake, the GM will call for a **test of Wands**.

- Success on this test moves the character’s Disposition to an adjacent, beneficial emotion or increases their current emotion’s severity.

- Failure moves the character’s Disposition towards a negative emotion.

title: Role-playing Disposition
body:
There are seven basic Dispositions: **anger, distaste, sadness, joy, surprise, trust, and fear**. Each of the seven Dispositions are listed below, with the core emotional state of each flanked by its mild and intense states. A list of emotional synonyms is also given, as one of those terms might be more appropriate and might aid in the GM in appropriately role-playing the Disposition. Some notes are also given as to how a creature with that Disposition might act in a Challenge.

### Acceptance | Trust | Admiration

Trust is a measure of belief in the general honesty, fairness, or capability of the other party. A base level of trust is a common starting Disposition for many benevolent creatures. Creatures who trust the guild will generally negotiate in good faith, but will still cautiously ensure the exchanges are fair. Betraying the trust of a character is a good way to change their Disposition to sad or angry.

**Synonyms:** confident, hopeful, optimistic, playful, interested, inquisitive, curious

In a **Challenge:** Typically, creatures with this Disposition are not inclined to fight. If the situation obligates a fight without changing the trust Disposition, the creature might attempt to learn more about the guild’s prowess through non-lethal methods.

### Annoyance | Anger | Rage

Anger is an intense emotional response that arises from a perceived provocation, threat, or hurt. Displays of anger are very aggressive and intimidating, and might quickly devolve to violence. It is a common emotional response for creatures with bestial intelligence or maladjusted humans. Anger is one half of the fight or flight response. Anger can impair the creature’s ability to take in information or make wise decisions during the encounter.

**Synonyms:** hurt, humiliated, threatened, hateful, violated, furious, provoked, hostile, ridiculed

In a **Challenge:** Anger makes people stupid and clumsy. The angry creature will try and focus on the source of their anger. An angry creature will attack recklessly, with little regard for the environment.

### Pensiveness | Sadness | Grief

Sadness is emotional pain associated with loss, despair, helplessness, or disappointment. Sad creatures often have obvious needs to be alleviated, which might change their Disposition for the better. However, sadness often causes creatures to lose interest in activities they once enjoyed, and sadness can create a significant barrier to positive influences.

**Synonyms:** anxious, empty, helpless, hopeless, depressed, irritable, guilty, lonely, abandoned

In a **Challenge:** In battle, those afflicted with deep sadness fight with abandon. They take chances they might otherwise not take. Often, they attempt to move first in Initiative, recklessly charging into battle and exposing themselves to danger.

### Boredom | Distaste | Loathing

Disgust is a reaction to something offensive, distasteful, or unpleasant. This revulsion is often a product of breaking hygiene norms or moral codes. It is a common starting Disposition for potentially antagonistic creatures you encounter. Remember, the adventuring life is a dirty, dirty business.

**Synonyms:** disapproving, repelled, judgmental, appalled, nauseated, horrified, hesitant

In a **Challenge:** Creatures full of loathing delight in violence against the targets of its distaste. The creature’s main desire is to cause harm or pain. This harm might be centered on a particular creature type (a witch-hunter pursuing a witch), or perhaps it’s more general (a vampire’s general disdain for all mortal life).

### Anxiety | Fear | Terror

Fear is an emotional response to a perceived danger or threat. Fear is one half of the flight-or-fight response. Creatures responding with fear often want to just end the social encounter and might make any concessions necessary to accomplish this. Or, if they think they can do so successfully, frightened creatures will try and abandon the encounter altogether.

**Synonyms:** weak, rejected, threatened, exposed, nervous, persecuted, inferior, worried, helpless

In a **Challenge:** Fearful creatures will attempt to flee the source of their fear, avoiding combat unless it is necessary to escape. They prioritize high-value cards for their Initiative.

### Distraction | Surprise | Awe

When there is a **disconnect** between expectations and reality, a creature reacts with surprise. Surprise might come when the guild interacts with the more “normal” society of the City—not everyone is accustomed to the adventurer’s life. Surprise might also occur during confusing or bewildering encounters in the Underworld.

**Synonyms:** startled, confused, amazed, shocked, dismayed, perplexed, excited

In a **Challenge:** A surprised creature wasn’t planning on fighting today. It will fight if it believes itself threatened, but won’t pursue combat for its own purposes. It will try to disengage as early as possible.

### Contentment | Joy | Ecstasy

When their needs are met, creatures feel a sense of joy or happiness. Like anger, feelings of joy can cloud judgment. This is the ideal state for influencing a creature, as they are well-disposed to entreaties and exchanges.

**Synonyms:** happy, peaceful, intimate, aroused, proud, thankful, powerful, respected

In a **Challenge:** Creatures who are joyful will not usually desire to engage in conflict. However, if the situation calls for it, joyful creatures might be cocky or overbold, perceiving the combat as a game. Cocky creatures might toy with, taunt, or tease adventurers during battle.

title: Example social encounter
body:
